data.name: Rita
data.long_meaning: In Latin, Rita is derived from the name Mara, meaning 'bitter'. However, in Christianity, it is believed to have evolved from the name of the Saint Mara or St. Mary Magdalene, who was often represented as holding a pearl, symbolizing her tears and her conversion from a sinful life. In this sense, Rita can be seen as a symbol of redemption and renewal.

in_greek.name: Ρίτα
in_greek.meaning: Η Ρίτα σημαίνει μαργαρίτα ή πολύτιμος λίθος
in_greek.long_meaning: Το όνομα Ρίτα προέρχεται από το λατινικό όνομα 'Margarita' που σημαίνει μαργαρίτα ή πολύτιμος λίθος. Το όνομα Margarita προέρχεται από το ελληνικό όνομα 'Μαργαρίτης' που αναφέρεται στο λίθο που ονομάζεται μαργαρίτης. Στην Καινή Διαθήκη, ο όνομα Margarita δεν αναφέρεται, αλλά το όνομα Ρίτα έχει χρησιμοποιηθεί στην Εκκλησία από τους πρώτους χρόνους.

historical_references.reference: According to Catholic tradition, Saint Rita of Cascia is the patron saint of impossible causes. Born in the late 13th or early 14th century in Rita de Cascia, Italy, she was married to a man who was violent and abusive. After his death, she joined an Augustinian monastery and dedicated her life to prayer and penance. She is said to have brought rain to a drought-stricken region by carrying a thorn in her side as a sign of her suffering. She died in 1457.

Saint Rita of Seville, also known as Rita of Cascia to distinguish her from the more famous Italian saint, was a Visigothic noblewoman who lived in the 5th century in what is now Spain. She was married against her will to a man who was already married, and when he died, she entered a convent. She is known for her patience and her miracles, including one in which she caused a dead child to come back to life. She is the patron saint of difficult marriages and of lost causes.
